title: Can you structure these 17 profitability and revenue decline questions in two minutes each?
description: 17 profitability and revenue decline case prompts to structure in two minutes each, with model answers, where to start and the trap to avoid.
hook: The most common case type in interviews. Seventeen prompts, from ski resorts to grocers, to make the profit split second nature. Give yourself two minutes per prompt, then open the model and look for what you missed.
body:
1. A national bank's mortgage applications are down 20% this year. Why?

Show a model structure
  • Market: Total applications in the market: rates, house prices, transactions; Is everyone down 20%, or just us?
  • Our offer: Rates and fees vs rivals; Loan-to-value limits, product range
  • Channels: Brokers: are they placing less with us?; Online and branch: traffic, conversion
  • Process: Time to decision, approval rate (brokers avoid slow or strict lenders); Drop-off during the application

Where to start: The market first: if all banks are down 20%, it is not our problem to fix.

The trap: Jumping to marketing ideas before checking whether the whole market fell.

2. A ski resort's profits fell 40% after two warm winters.

Show a model structure
  • Winter revenue: Visitors × spend, by month; Lift passes, ski school, food, rentals
  • Costs: Fixed costs: lifts, staff, maintenance; Variable and snow-related: snowmaking, energy
  • Snow risk: Days open, altitude, snowmaking coverage; Trend or two bad years? Share of revenue pre-sold as season passes
  • Non-ski income: Summer, events, conferences; Year-round use of lifts, hotels and restaurants

Where to start: Days open: warm winters cut the season, and costs are mostly fixed.

The trap: Treating it as a normal profit decline and missing that weather is the root cause.

3. A pharma company's new drug is selling 40% below forecast.

Show a model structure
  • Doctors: Awareness and trust in the data; Who prescribes: specialists vs family doctors
  • Patients: How many are diagnosed and eligible; was the forecast realistic?; Price, side effects, stopping early
  • Payers: Approval for reimbursement; Restrictions: only after other drugs fail
  • Competition: Rival drugs and generics; Their pricing and contracts

Where to start: Payers: if insurers restrict it, doctors and patients can do little.

The trap: Assuming it is a marketing problem when access and reimbursement usually decide.

4. A cinema chain's attendance is still 25% below pre-pandemic levels.

Show a model structure
  • Market: Total cinema attendance vs ours; Film supply: fewer big releases?
  • Our offer: Ticket and snack prices; Comfort, screens, locations
  • Substitutes: Streaming windows shorter; Home viewing habits
  • Customers: Which groups have not come back; Frequency vs number of visitors

Where to start: Market vs us: are we below the industry, or is the whole market smaller?

The trap: Ignoring the supply of films, which drives most of the attendance.

5. A software company's customer churn has doubled to 2% a month.

Show a model structure
  • Who is leaving: By size, plan, age of account; New customers vs long-standing ones
  • Why they leave: Product gaps, bugs, price rise; Moved to a competitor or stopped needing it
  • When: After onboarding, at renewal, after a change; Any link to a recent release or price change
  • What we do about it: Onboarding and support; Contracts, pricing, success teams

Where to start: Who is leaving: churn is rarely spread evenly, so find the segment.

The trap: Jumping to retention discounts before knowing who leaves and why.

6. A grocer's operating margin fell from 4% to 2% in two years, while sales grew.

Show a model structure
  • Prices and mix: Discounting to match rivals; Shift to lower-margin categories
  • Cost of goods: Supplier prices, shrinkage and waste; Private label share
  • Store costs: Wages, energy, rent; Per store and per $ of sales
  • Online and delivery: Share of sales online; Cost to pick and deliver each order

Where to start: Sales grew but margin halved: find which cost grew faster than sales, as % of sales.

The trap: Talking about growing sales when the problem is margin.

7. A city hotel's revenue per available room fell 15% this year.

Show a model structure
  • Occupancy: Rooms sold vs rooms available; By segment: business, leisure, groups
  • Room rate: Average price per night vs rivals; Discounting and channel mix
  • Market: City demand: events, flights, offices; New hotels opened nearby
  • Channel mix: Visibility and ranking on booking sites; Direct bookings and corporate contracts

Where to start: Occupancy vs rate: find which one fell, then which segment, then whether the market or our position explains it.

The trap: Treating revenue per room as one number instead of occupancy × rate.

8. A casual-dining chain's profit per restaurant has halved in three years.

Show a model structure
  • Covers: Guests per restaurant per week; Lunch vs dinner, weekday vs weekend
  • Spend per guest: Menu prices, drinks, desserts; Discounts and vouchers
  • Food and drink costs: Ingredient prices, waste; Menu mix towards low-margin dishes
  • Restaurant costs: Staff hours and wages; Rent, energy, delivery fees

Where to start: Covers first: footfall drops usually drive most of a restaurant's profit fall.

The trap: Blaming food inflation without checking whether fewer people come in.

9. A car dealer group's profit fell 30% even though it sold more cars.

Show a model structure
  • New cars: Margin per car, maker bonuses; Discounts to hit targets
  • Used cars: Volume, price, time on the lot; Stock bought at the peak
  • Finance and insurance: Share of buyers taking finance; Commission per deal
  • Service and parts: Workshop hours sold; Customers returning for servicing
  • Costs: Interest on stock financing, staff; Property and marketing

Where to start: Profit by business line, then costs: dealers make most of their profit from used cars, finance and servicing, not new cars.

The trap: Looking only at new-car sales, where dealers earn least.

10. A shopping app's conversion from visit to purchase fell from 4% to 3%.

Show a model structure
  • Traffic mix: New vs returning visitors; Source: ads, search, social
  • Funnel step: Product page, basket, checkout, payment; Where the drop-off grew
  • Offer: Prices, stock, delivery cost and time; Rivals' promotions
  • Technical: App release, speed, payment errors; Device or browser

Where to start: Traffic mix: cheaper ads often bring visitors who were never going to buy.

The trap: Redesigning checkout before checking whether the visitors changed.

11. A car insurer's claims costs rose 25% in a year while customer numbers were flat.

Show a model structure
  • Number of claims: Claims per 1,000 policies; Accidents, theft, weather
  • Cost per claim: Repair costs, parts, labour rates; Hire cars, injury payouts
  • Customer mix: Younger drivers, riskier areas; Pricing that attracted bad risks
  • Fraud and process: Suspicious claims; Claims handling and supplier contracts

Where to start: Frequency vs severity: are there more claims, or does each cost more?

The trap: Raising prices across the board before knowing which customers cost more.

12. A meal-kit company acquires plenty of customers but still loses money.

Show a model structure
  • Cost to acquire: Marketing spend per new customer; Discounts on first boxes
  • How long they stay: Churn after the discount ends; Orders per customer
  • Margin per box: Price, ingredients, packaging; Delivery and picking costs
  • Fixed costs: Kitchens and warehouses; Tech and head office

Where to start: How long they stay: if most leave after the discount, acquisition is wasted.

The trap: Celebrating customer growth without checking what each customer is worth.

13. A consulting firm's consultants billed 62% of their time this year, down from 75%.

Show a model structure
  • Demand: New projects sold, pipeline; Client budgets and sector mix
  • Supply: Hiring ahead of demand; Fewer people leaving than planned
  • Matching: Right skills in the wrong place; Staffing process, gaps between projects
  • Non-billable time: Internal work, proposals, training; How time is recorded

Where to start: Demand vs supply: did sales fall, or did headcount grow faster than sales?

The trap: Cutting training before checking whether the firm simply over-hired.

14. A gym chain loses 50% of new members within six months.

Show a model structure
  • When they leave: First three months after joining; After a promotional price ends
  • Who leaves: Joined via discount, age, goals; Visit frequency in the first month
  • Experience: Crowding, cleanliness, classes; Onboarding and personal contact
  • Price and contract: Price vs nearby rivals; Ease of cancelling

Where to start: Visit frequency in the first month: members who don't build a habit leave.

The trap: Offering bigger joining discounts, which bring in more people likely to leave.

15. A shampoo brand has lost 4 points of market share in a year.

Show a model structure
  • Where share went: To which rivals or own-label; Which channels and stores
  • Price: Our price gap vs rivals; Promotions frequency
  • Product and brand: New launches by rivals; Advertising and awareness
  • Distribution: Shelf space, out of stocks; Online visibility

Where to start: Where the share went: losing to own-label is a price problem, to a rival launch a product problem.

The trap: Spending more on advertising before knowing who took the share.

16. A dairy cooperative's margin fell from 8% to 3% while milk volumes grew.

Show a model structure
  • Milk price paid to farmers: Price per litre vs market; Commitments in contracts
  • Product mix: Cheese, butter, liquid milk, powder; Shift to low-value products
  • Selling prices: Supermarket contracts; Export prices and currency
  • Processing costs: Energy, packaging, transport; Plant utilisation

Where to start: Milk price paid vs selling prices: a co-op is squeezed between the two, and may choose to pay its farmer-owners more.

The trap: Pushing volume, which adds more low-margin milk.

17. How can a car maker raise its operating margin from 4% to 8%?

Show a model structure
  • Price and mix: More premium models, fewer discounts; Options and features
  • Material costs: Platform sharing, fewer parts; Supplier negotiations
  • Manufacturing: Plant utilisation, closing plants; Automation
  • Overheads: R&D focus, fewer models; Sales and marketing

Where to start: Price and mix: fewer discounts often add more margin than cost cuts.

The trap: Only cutting costs.
